items.label: f01-position-key
items.front: Progress is stored in each learner's localStorage under `stepKey(stageId, moduleId, index)`, documented as 'A stable id for one step'. The team plans to re-sequence the roadmap JSON. Evidence: the v1 stepKey quoted in case study 09:26-31. What is the risk?
items.back: The key encodes position, so any insert, delete or move silently shifts or orphans ticks in every browser at once, and nothing throws. Fix: derive the key from what the step points at (`module/kind:target`), enforce its uniqueness in the build, and migrate old keys once through a frozen map.

items.label: f12-queue-vs-topic-naming
items.front: `OrderPlaced` goes onto a work queue that the email, analytics and search services all consume from, and each service sees only some of the orders. Another message, `SendInvoiceEmail`, is published to a topic. Evidence: system-design-lite.json sd-065, sd-066. What is wrong?
items.back: A work queue hands each message to one of its competing consumers, so the three services are splitting the orders between them; fan-out needs a pub/sub topic, where every subscriber gets its own copy. Names show intent: `OrderPlaced` is an event, a past-tense fact anyone may react to; `SendInvoiceEmail` is a command for one handler, so it belongs on a queue.

items.label: f04-backup-without-restore
items.front: On first load after the v2 release, read() stores the raw v1 payload under `devpath.progress.v1.backup` and overwrites the main key with migrated v2 state. Evidence: progress.ts:336-347; the decision record notes nothing restores the backup. What does that mean if a mapping turns out wrong?
items.back: The rollback data exists but is unreachable: a learner whose ticks were mis-mapped can't get them back without hand-editing localStorage (LT-10). Fix: ship and test a restore path (e.g. a Settings action that re-runs migrate() from the backup with a corrected table).

items.label: f09-webhook-timestamp-verify-store
items.front: A payment-webhook endpoint checks an HMAC over the body only, then fulfils the whole order inline, emails included, before it replies. Evidence: system-design-lite.json sd-094, sd-095. What two problems does this create?
items.back: An HMAC over the body proves who sent it, not when, so a captured request can be replayed forever and still verify: sign a timestamp too and reject anything older than a few minutes. Doing the work inline makes the reply slow, so the provider times out and retries, and orders get fulfilled twice. Fix: verify, store the event, return 2xx quickly, and let a background job do the work.

items.label: f07-rpo-rto-untested-backups
items.front: A team states an RPO of one hour. Its only protection is a nightly database backup that has run for a year and has never been restored. Evidence: system-design-lite.json sd-106, sd-107. What two gaps does this hide?
items.back: RPO is how much recent data you may lose, so one hour needs backups or replication at least hourly; a nightly backup can lose up to 24 hours. And an unrestored backup is unproven: it may be corrupt or incomplete, and nobody knows the restore time that the RTO (how fast you must be running again) depends on. Fix: back up to match the RPO and schedule timed test restores.

items.label: f13-thin-events-callback
items.front: `OrderPlaced` carries only the order id, and each of five consumers calls the orders API for the details. During a sale the orders API slows down, and a consumer that is running late records a cancelled order. Evidence: system-design-lite.json sd-068. What is the design trade-off?
items.back: A thin event forces a callback: 1,000 events × 5 consumers is 5,000 API calls, and a late consumer sees the order as it is now, not as it was when the event was raised. Fat events carry the facts at the time, at the cost of larger messages and a payload contract to version. Choose per event; neither shape is always right.

items.label: f06-money-integer-pence
items.front: A checkout stores prices in a floating-point column and adds basket lines up in floating point. Finance reports order totals that are a penny out now and then. Evidence: system-design-lite.json sd-108. What is going on?
items.back: 0.10 has no exact binary representation, so sums of prices drift by fractions of a penny (0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004) and totals stop reconciling. Fix: store money as `decimal(12,2)` or as integer minor units (pence), with a currency code, and do the arithmetic in those exact types.

items.label: f11-holds-expire-as-data
items.front: A ticketing app holds a seat for 10 minutes with a timer in the web server's memory, and after a deploy some seats stay blocked. When a seat frees up on a sold-out show, everyone on the waitlist is emailed at once. Evidence: system-design-lite.json sd-052, sd-120. What should change?
items.back: Server timers vanish on restart, so make expiry data: a hold row with `expires_at` that availability queries ignore once it has passed; a clean-up job can delete old rows later without correctness depending on it. Reuse the same pattern for the waitlist: offer the place to the next person with a timed hold, and move down the list if it lapses, instead of starting a race.

items.label: f10-webhook-event-unique
items.front: A provider re-sends a payment webhook because your 2xx came late. Your handler inserts every delivery into `webhook_events` under a fresh row id and then fulfils it, so the order ships twice. Evidence: system-design-lite.json sd-140. What is missing?
items.back: Nothing marks the retried delivery as the same event. Put a unique constraint on `(provider, event_id)`: the second insert of that event fails, and the handler treats the failure as 'already handled' and skips the work. The provider's event id is the identity; your own row id is new on every delivery, so it can never catch a repeat.

items.label: f16-status-state-machine
items.front: An order has `isPaid`, `isShipped` and `isCancelled` booleans, and support keeps finding orders that are both shipped and cancelled. More unit tests were added and it still happens. Evidence: system-design-lite.json sd-057. Why, and what is the fix?
items.back: Three booleans allow 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 combinations, most of them nonsense, and every code path that sets one flag can create one. Replace them with a single status plus an explicit list of allowed transitions (pending to paid, paid to shipped, pending to cancelled), enforced in one place, so the invalid state cannot be stored at all. Tests and logs only detect it.

items.label: f05-fan-out-on-write-celebrity
items.front: A Twitter-lite builds each home timeline at request time from the follows table. Reads now dominate, so the team plans to push every new post id into each follower's precomputed timeline instead. Evidence: system-design-for-crud.md:77-90. What does that switch cost, and what about an account with a million followers?
items.back: Fan-out on write turns each read into one cheap lookup but makes every post cost one write per follower: a million writes for one celebrity post. Fix: fan out on write for ordinary accounts, but fetch celebrity accounts' posts at read time and merge them into the precomputed timeline.

items.label: f15-monthly-partitions-drop
items.front: An `events` table grows by 50 million rows a month, queries touch only the last 90 days, and a nightly DELETE of rows older than 90 days now runs for hours and bloats the table. Evidence: system-design-lite.json sd-131, sd-119. What is the cheaper design?
items.back: Partition the table by month: retiring a month becomes one detach or drop of a partition, a metadata operation, instead of deleting 50 million rows that then need vacuuming, and date-filtered queries skip old partitions. Costs: a unique constraint must include the partition key, and updates across months get no cheaper. Archiving old rows elsewhere is the simpler alternative.

items.label: f14-sticky-sessions-stopgap
items.front: Sessions live in each server's memory, so the load balancer pins every user to one server. Evidence: system-design-lite.json sd-042. What happens on the next deploy, and when a few users are much busier than the rest?
items.back: Each restart or crash logs out everyone pinned to that server, and busy users pile onto whichever server they happened to land on while others idle. Stickiness is a stopgap: keep session data where every instance can read it (Redis, the database, or a signed cookie), and the balancer can send any request anywhere.

items.label: f03-unguarded-new-keys
items.front: A step added after v2 (e.g. `js/86-sqlite-orders` in `m-sql`) has its target changed in place. The only key guard is a test that checks the 195 v1 legacy-table values exist on the roadmap. Evidence: types.ts:150-161, selectors.test.ts:64-76. What breaks?
items.back: The step gets a new key and every learner's tick on the old key is orphaned silently, while `npm run content` and `npm test` still pass. Fix (LT-15): snapshot all current step keys and fail the content build when a key disappears without a mapping entry that migrate() applies.

items.label: f02-effect-in-updater
items.front: A countdown calls `setLeft((value) => { … expire.current(); return 0; })` and the app runs under StrictMode in development. Evidence: postmortem timeline (2026-09-09 entry). What happens when a question times out?
items.back: React calls the impure updater twice, so the question is graded twice: two lapses, ease down 0.4 instead of 0.2, two log rows, all persisted. Fix: keep updaters pure — fire expiry from the interval callback behind a `fired` ref, and mount the test harness under StrictMode.

items.label: f08-three-nines-error-budget
items.front: A service promises 99.9% availability, and each weekly release is a manual deploy that takes the site down for about 10 minutes. Evidence: system-design-lite.json sd-105, sd-127. Does that fit the target, and what should happen when the month's allowance runs out?
items.back: 0.1% of a 30-day month (43,200 minutes) is about 43 minutes, and four 10-minute deploys spend about 40 of them, leaving almost nothing for real incidents. That allowance is the error budget: while it lasts the team ships freely; once it is spent, work shifts to reliability. Fix: zero-downtime deploys, or a target the release process can actually meet.

items.prompt: A customer double-clicks "Place order" and two identical `POST /orders` requests arrive. What is the standard server-side protection?

choices.text: Disable the button after the first click and rely on the client
Reject any second order from the same customer within one minute
Deduplicate orders by comparing basket contents in a nightly job
Accept an `Idempotency-Key` header and replay the first response

choices: Disable the button after the first click and rely on the client
Reject any second order from the same customer within one minute
Deduplicate orders by comparing basket contents in a nightly job
Accept an `Idempotency-Key` header and replay the first response

items.explanation: The client generates one key per checkout attempt and sends it on every retry of that attempt; the server stores the key with the result and returns the stored response for any repeat, so the double click creates one order and both requests get the same answer. Disabling the button helps, but it is client-side only: network retries and replayed requests bypass it. Rejecting any second order within a minute also blocks a customer who genuinely orders twice. A nightly clean-up comes after the card has already been charged twice.

items.prompt: migrate() maps each v1 tick with `LEGACY[oldKey] ?? oldKey`. What is the consequence of keeping unknown keys verbatim instead of dropping them?

choices.text: History is kept, since orphan ticks stay hidden but survive export and import
The build fails until each unknown key gets its own entry in the legacy table
Unknown keys count toward module completion, inflating learners' progress
Unknown keys are re-attached to their module's first step on the next render

choices: History is kept, since orphan ticks stay hidden but survive export and import
The build fails until each unknown key gets its own entry in the legacy table
Unknown keys count toward module completion, inflating learners' progress
Unknown keys are re-attached to their module's first step on the next render

items.explanation: No step renders an unmapped key, but nothing is thrown away, so the orphan ticks can still be recovered; an earlier draft dropped them and F-21 recorded the change.

items.prompt: Your CDN caches `GET /api/me/orders`, and users start seeing each other's orders. What went wrong?

choices.text: A per-user response was cacheable by shared caches; it needs `private` or `no-store`
The API returned an ETag, and matching ETags let the CDN swap users' responses
The CDN's edge servers share a disk, so all users on one edge location read the same stored file
The CDN's TTL was too long; a TTL under a minute would keep each user's data apart

choices: A per-user response was cacheable by shared caches; it needs `private` or `no-store`
The API returned an ETag, and matching ETags let the CDN swap users' responses
The CDN's edge servers share a disk, so all users on one edge location read the same stored file
The CDN's TTL was too long; a TTL under a minute would keep each user's data apart

items.explanation: Shared caches such as a CDN key on the URL, and `/api/me/orders` is the same URL for every user, so one user's stored response is served to whoever asks next. A personal response must say `Cache-Control: private` (only that user's browser may store it) or `no-store` (nobody may). A short TTL just leaks for less time: even 30 seconds hands one user's orders to everyone in that window. An ETag lets a cache revalidate the copy it already has; it never swaps one user's response for another's. Edge servers sharing a disk is not the cause: the CDN stored the response under its URL exactly as the headers allowed.

items.prompt: In SQS, a message's visibility timeout is 30 seconds, but processing sometimes takes 45. What happens?

choices.text: The message becomes visible again and a second consumer processes it too
The message moves straight to the dead-letter queue as a failure
The broker cancels the consumer's work after 30 seconds
Nothing, because the timeout only applies before the first delivery

choices: The message becomes visible again and a second consumer processes it too
The message moves straight to the dead-letter queue as a failure
The broker cancels the consumer's work after 30 seconds
Nothing, because the timeout only applies before the first delivery

items.explanation: While a consumer works, the message is hidden; if it is not deleted before the timeout, the broker assumes the consumer died and makes it visible again. With a 30-second timeout and a 45-second job, the message reappears at second 30, a second consumer takes it, and both finish: it is processed twice. The fix is a timeout longer than the slowest job (or extending it while working), plus an idempotent consumer. The broker cannot stop your code mid-run; one expired timeout does not dead-letter a message (that takes repeated receives up to a maximum count); and the timeout applies to every receive, not only before the first.

items.prompt: A popular cache key expires, and hundreds of concurrent requests miss at once and all query the database. What prevents this stampede?

choices.text: Let one request rebuild the value while the others wait for it or get the stale copy
Shorten the TTL, so each expiry releases a smaller burst of requests on the database
Add a read replica, so the burst of identical queries is spread over two databases
Give the key a longer TTL, so the database is hit less often when it does expire

choices: Let one request rebuild the value while the others wait for it or get the stale copy
Shorten the TTL, so each expiry releases a smaller burst of requests on the database
Add a read replica, so the burst of identical queries is spread over two databases
Give the key a longer TTL, so the database is hit less often when it does expire

items.explanation: Request coalescing (a lock or single-flight per key), serving the stale copy while one caller refreshes, or refreshing early with jitter all make one query do the work of hundreds: 500 concurrent misses become 1 database query instead of 500. A longer TTL only makes the stampede rarer; when the key does expire, all 500 still miss together. A shorter TTL makes it more frequent, not smaller, because the burst size is set by how many requests arrive while the key is missing. A read replica spreads the same 500 queries over two servers, about 250 each: it halves the burst instead of removing it.

items.prompt: A downstream service is timing out, and your retries are making its recovery harder. What does a circuit breaker add?

choices.text: After repeated failures it fails fast for a cool-off period instead of calling
It retries each failed call straight away, several times, until one succeeds
It routes the calls to a cached copy of the service kept on the calling side
It raises the timeout on each call, so slow responses stop counting as failures

choices: After repeated failures it fails fast for a cool-off period instead of calling
It retries each failed call straight away, several times, until one succeeds
It routes the calls to a cached copy of the service kept on the calling side
It raises the timeout on each call, so slow responses stop counting as failures

items.explanation: Once failures pass a threshold the breaker opens and calls fail immediately for a cool-off period; then a trial call tests recovery, which closes the breaker on success and reopens it on failure. That stops your retries piling onto a struggling service and frees your own threads. Immediate repeated retries are the problem the question describes: with four retries each, every caller sends five times the load. A longer timeout makes each stuck call hold a thread longer. A cached copy of the service is a fallback you may add, not what a breaker is. Pair the breaker with timeouts, backoff and a fallback where you have one.

items.prompt: Before the fix, answer() returned early when `chosen !== undefined`. Why did that guard not stop the second grade under StrictMode?

choices.text: The timer called a different answer function than the click handler did
setChosen is asynchronous, so the guard ran before React scheduled the update
StrictMode resets the component's state between its two invocations
Both calls closed over the same render's chosen, which was still undefined

choices: The timer called a different answer function than the click handler did
setChosen is asynchronous, so the guard ran before React scheduled the update
StrictMode resets the component's state between its two invocations
Both calls closed over the same render's chosen, which was still undefined

items.explanation: State does not change inside one render's closure: a state guard protects against a second render, not two calls in one. The fix adds a ref (`answeredIndex`) that is read live, plus moves expiry out of the updater.

items.prompt: The v2 key is `module/kind:target`. Why can't it drop the module and use a global `kind:target`?

choices.text: Without the module, the key would exceed the localStorage key-length limit
Removing the module would make inserting a step move learners' ticks again
Several modules reuse one drill deck, so a global key would merge their ticks
Targets repeat even within one module, so the module prefix disambiguates them

choices: Without the module, the key would exceed the localStorage key-length limit
Removing the module would make inserting a step move learners' ticks again
Several modules reuse one drill deck, so a global key would merge their ticks
Targets repeat even within one module, so the module prefix disambiguates them

items.explanation: kind:target is unique within a module (the build enforces it) but not across modules: 7 decks were reused on the v1 roadmap and 24 targets are shared today.

items.prompt: Your queue delivers at least once, and a 'charge card' message is occasionally processed twice. What is the standard fix?

choices.text: Acknowledge the message before processing, so it can never be delivered again
Make the consumer idempotent, for example by recording processed message ids
Switch the queue to exactly-once mode, which removes every duplicate on the broker
Delay each charge briefly so the duplicate arrives first and can be dropped

choices: Acknowledge the message before processing, so it can never be delivered again
Make the consumer idempotent, for example by recording processed message ids
Switch the queue to exactly-once mode, which removes every duplicate on the broker
Delay each charge briefly so the duplicate arrives first and can be dropped

items.explanation: At-least-once delivery plus an idempotent consumer gives effectively-once effects: store each processed message id (an insert that fails on a repeat), or pass an idempotency key to the payment provider, and skip repeats. No broker setting removes every duplicate end to end; brokers that advertise exactly-once mean deduplication within a window or inside their own system. Acknowledging before processing turns delivery into at-most-once, so a crash after the ack loses the charge entirely. A short delay cannot tell which copy is the duplicate, and nothing guarantees which copy arrives first.

items.prompt: One slow downstream API ties up every worker thread in your service, so requests that never call it also time out. Which pattern contains this?

choices.text: A bulkhead: a separate, capped pool for calls to that API
Sticky sessions, so slow users stay on one server only
A larger global thread pool, so there are spare threads
A read replica, so slow calls go to a different database

choices: A bulkhead: a separate, capped pool for calls to that API
Sticky sessions, so slow users stay on one server only
A larger global thread pool, so there are spare threads
A read replica, so slow calls go to a different database

items.explanation: A bulkhead limits how many concurrent calls may go to one dependency, say 10 of 200 worker threads, so when that API slows only those 10 fill up and that feature queues or fails, while the other 190 keep serving everything else. A bigger global pool fills up too, just later: if the slow API holds each thread for 30 seconds, more threads only delay the moment all of them are waiting. A read replica moves database reads, not outbound API calls. Sticky sessions pin users to servers and do nothing about threads stuck waiting on another service.

items.prompt: In a shared-schema multi-tenant app, each tenant's users need unique email addresses. Which constraint is right?

choices.text: `UNIQUE (email)` across the whole users table
`UNIQUE (tenant_id)` across the users table
No constraint; check for duplicates in the API
`UNIQUE (tenant_id, email)` on the users table

choices: `UNIQUE (email)` across the whole users table
`UNIQUE (tenant_id)` across the users table
No constraint; check for duplicates in the API
`UNIQUE (tenant_id, email)` on the users table

items.explanation: The same person may belong to two customer organisations, so email is unique within a tenant, not globally. With `UNIQUE (tenant_id, email)`, alice@example.com can exist once in tenant 1 and once in tenant 2, but not twice in tenant 1. A global `UNIQUE (email)` blocks her second organisation. `UNIQUE (tenant_id)` allows only one user per tenant. A check in the API alone loses to two concurrent inserts: both requests look, both find no duplicate, both insert.

items.prompt: The UX review proposed `stage/module/kind:target`. What did leaving the stage out buy, and what had to be enforced in exchange?

choices.text: Faster progress-map lookups, in exchange for forbidding modules to share a deck
No functional gain; the stage was dropped just because the URL already holds it
Shorter keys in exported files, in exchange for a migration whenever a stage is renamed
Modules can change stage with no key change; the build rejects duplicate module ids

choices: Faster progress-map lookups, in exchange for forbidding modules to share a deck
No functional gain; the stage was dropped just because the URL already holds it
Shorter keys in exported files, in exchange for a migration whenever a stage is renamed
Modules can change stage with no key change; the build rejects duplicate module ids

items.explanation: Leaving the stage out lets modules move between stages without changing any key, in exchange for the build failing on duplicate module ids. Module ids are globally unique, so the stage adds only fragility; three modules moved stage in the same change without touching a key. validateRoadmap reports a module id used in two stages.

items.prompt: Uploads go to storage first and are confirmed later, and some users abandon them. How do you stop orphaned files piling up?

choices.text: Delete the file whenever the browser tab closes during the upload
Run a monthly job that deletes any object older than thirty days
Give every object a public URL so that users can clean up their own abandoned files
Write uploads under a `pending/` prefix and let a lifecycle rule expire them

choices: Delete the file whenever the browser tab closes during the upload
Run a monthly job that deletes any object older than thirty days
Give every object a public URL so that users can clean up their own abandoned files
Write uploads under a `pending/` prefix and let a lifecycle rule expire them

items.explanation: Unconfirmed uploads land under a temporary prefix; confirming copies or moves the object to its final key, and a bucket lifecycle rule deletes anything still under `pending/` after a day, with no job of yours to keep running. A browser cannot be relied on to report closing: a crash, a dead battery or a lost connection sends nothing. A sweep of every object older than thirty days also deletes real, confirmed files, because age alone does not say whether an upload was confirmed. Public URLs make the files readable by anyone and still rely on users to tidy up, which they will not do.

items.prompt: gen-legacy-step-keys.mjs exits with an error if its output exists, unless `--force` is passed. Why is re-running it against today's roadmap harmful?

choices.text: The script edits content/roadmap.json in place, so a second run corrupts it
A second run doubles each entry, so migrate() would apply each mapping twice
Regenerating would reorder the JSON keys and create a noisy diff in code review
Old ticks follow the 2220491 roadmap's positions; a new map would misroute them

choices: The script edits content/roadmap.json in place, so a second run corrupts it
A second run doubles each entry, so migrate() would apply each mapping twice
Regenerating would reorder the JSON keys and create a noisy diff in code review
Old ticks follow the 2220491 roadmap's positions; a new map would misroute them

items.explanation: Position n in module m only means something in the roadmap that v1 shipped with. A map generated from the edited roadmap would send old ticks to the wrong steps. The map is frozen history; a regenerated one 'would describe the new roadmap, not the one old progress was written against'.

items.prompt: One malformed message makes the consumer throw every time, and the queue keeps redelivering it. What should the consumer setup do?

choices.text: Retry it forever with exponential backoff, since the bug will eventually be fixed
Restart the consumer process after each failure, which clears the bad state
Cap delivery attempts, then move the message to a dead-letter queue and alert
Delete it silently on the first failure, so it can never block the queue again

choices: Retry it forever with exponential backoff, since the bug will eventually be fixed
Restart the consumer process after each failure, which clears the bad state
Cap delivery attempts, then move the message to a dead-letter queue and alert
Delete it silently on the first failure, so it can never block the queue again

items.explanation: A poison message fails every time, so unbounded retries waste capacity and, on an ordered queue, block every message behind it. Capping attempts (say five) and then moving the message to a dead-letter queue keeps it for diagnosis, and the alert makes sure someone looks. Retrying forever cannot succeed until a person fixes the bug, so it only burns capacity meanwhile. Deleting on the first failure also throws away messages that failed for a transient reason such as a timeout. Restarting the process does not change the message, so the next delivery fails the same way.

items.prompt: Option (a) would rekey v1 progress in ContentGate once the roadmap had been fetched. Why was a shape-only migrate() over a frozen table chosen instead?

choices.text: Fetching the roadmap requires a server, which this local-first app does not have
ContentGate renders on each navigation, so the rekey would run again and again
A frozen table ships smaller than the code needed to walk the fetched roadmap
Rekeying reads old positions through the new roadmap, which loads after progress

choices: Fetching the roadmap requires a server, which this local-first app does not have
ContentGate renders on each navigation, so the rekey would run again and again
A frozen table ships smaller than the code needed to walk the fetched roadmap
Rekeying reads old positions through the new roadmap, which loads after progress

items.explanation: progress.ts loads synchronously at import time and content arrives later by fetch, so the roadmap is not even available when progress is read; worse, mapping through the edited roadmap is exactly wrong once steps have moved.

items.prompt: One tenant's nightly export saturates the shared database and slows every other tenant. What handles this noisy neighbour without buying capacity for one tenant's peak?

choices.text: Separate login pages per tenant, so their traffic arrives through different routes
Per-tenant quotas and rate limits, with heavy exports moved to a queue and a replica
An index on tenant_id, so every tenant's queries run faster regardless of load
A larger database instance, so there is always spare capacity for every tenant

choices: Separate login pages per tenant, so their traffic arrives through different routes
Per-tenant quotas and rate limits, with heavy exports moved to a queue and a replica
An index on tenant_id, so every tenant's queries run faster regardless of load
A larger database instance, so there is always spare capacity for every tenant

items.explanation: Isolate the heavy workload instead of sizing for it: throttle each tenant, and run exports as background jobs that read from a replica, so they cannot starve interactive traffic on the primary. A bigger instance buys time only until the next export grows, and you pay all month for one tenant's nightly peak. An index on tenant_id speeds up filtering but does nothing to stop one tenant using most of the CPU and disk. Separate login pages change only how requests arrive; every tenant's queries still land on the same database. Very large tenants may eventually get a database of their own.

items.prompt: When read() finds a v1 payload, it saves a backup only if none exists and immediately writes the migrated v2 state back to storage. What does that ordering guarantee?

choices.text: Each reload refreshes the backup with the latest v1 data before it migrates
Storage keeps both versions live, and the app reads whichever one is newer
The first raw v1 payload stays the rollback copy, and reloads read v2 directly
The migrated state is written back once the learner confirms the upgrade prompt

choices: Each reload refreshes the backup with the latest v1 data before it migrates
Storage keeps both versions live, and the app reads whichever one is newer
The first raw v1 payload stays the rollback copy, and reloads read v2 directly
The migrated state is written back once the learner confirms the upgrade prompt

items.explanation: `if (localStorage.getItem(V1_BACKUP_KEY) === null)` keeps the first raw v1 string; writing v2 under the same key means a reload neither migrates nor backs up again. A failed write leaves correct in-memory state and retries on the next commit.

items.prompt: What is the difference between cache-aside and write-through caching?

choices.text: Cache-aside fills the cache on a read miss; write-through updates the cache on every write
Cache-aside keeps the cache on a separate server; write-through keeps it inside the database
Cache-aside never expires its entries; write-through expires them as soon as the row changes
Cache-aside buffers writes until a batch is flushed; write-through sends each write straight on

choices: Cache-aside fills the cache on a read miss; write-through updates the cache on every write
Cache-aside keeps the cache on a separate server; write-through keeps it inside the database
Cache-aside never expires its entries; write-through expires them as soon as the row changes
Cache-aside buffers writes until a batch is flushed; write-through sends each write straight on

items.explanation: Cache-aside loads lazily: the app checks the cache, and only on a miss reads the database and stores the result, so only data someone actually reads gets cached, and an entry stays stale until it is invalidated or expires. Write-through updates the cache as part of every write, so it stays fresh, at the cost of caching data nobody reads. Where the cache runs is not what separates the two, and neither pattern rules out a TTL. Buffering writes and flushing them later in a batch is a third pattern, write-behind: fast, but writes are lost if the cache dies before the flush.

items.prompt: You save an order, then publish an OrderPlaced event; if the process dies between the two, the event is lost. What does the outbox pattern do?

choices.text: Wraps the database write and the broker publish together in one two-phase commit
Publishes the event first and saves the order only once the broker confirms receipt
Retries the publish in a loop inside the request until the broker finally accepts it
Saves the event in an outbox table in the same transaction; a relay publishes it later

choices: Wraps the database write and the broker publish together in one two-phase commit
Publishes the event first and saves the order only once the broker confirms receipt
Retries the publish in a loop inside the request until the broker finally accepts it
Saves the event in an outbox table in the same transaction; a relay publishes it later

items.explanation: The order row and an outbox row are written in one database transaction, so they commit or roll back together, and a separate relay reads the outbox and publishes, retrying until the broker accepts. The relay can publish twice (a crash after publishing, before it marks the row done), so consumers stay idempotent. Publishing first just moves the gap: if the save then fails, an event exists for an order that does not. Two-phase commit across a database and a broker is exactly what the outbox avoids. A retry loop inside the request dies with the process, which is the failure the question starts from.

items.prompt: You need to rename the `customers.fullname` column to `display_name` while old and new app versions run side by side during a rolling deploy. What is the safe sequence?

choices.text: Add the new column, write both, backfill, switch reads, then drop the old one
Deploy the new app version first, then rename the column once all traffic has moved to it
Rename the column in one migration, then deploy the new app version
Take the site offline for five minutes and do both changes together

choices: Add the new column, write both, backfill, switch reads, then drop the old one
Deploy the new app version first, then rename the column once all traffic has moved to it
Rename the column in one migration, then deploy the new app version
Take the site offline for five minutes and do both changes together

items.explanation: Expand and contract keeps the schema compatible with both app versions at every step: add `display_name`, have the app write both columns, backfill the old rows, switch reads to the new column, and drop `fullname` only when no running version reads it. Renaming first breaks the old instances still reading `fullname`. Deploying the new version first breaks the new instances instead, because their queries name `display_name`, which does not exist yet. Five minutes offline works, but avoiding downtime is the whole point of a rolling deploy.

items.prompt: You scale from 4 to 40 app instances, each with a pool of 50 connections, and Postgres starts refusing connections. What is the usual fix?

choices.text: Remove the app-side pools so each request opens and closes its own connection
Add a read replica, so half of the connections go to a second database server
Put a pooler such as PgBouncer in front of Postgres and shrink each app pool
Raise the Postgres `max_connections` to 2,000 so every instance pool fits

choices: Remove the app-side pools so each request opens and closes its own connection
Add a read replica, so half of the connections go to a second database server
Put a pooler such as PgBouncer in front of Postgres and shrink each app pool
Raise the Postgres `max_connections` to 2,000 so every instance pool fits

items.explanation: Work the numbers: 4 instances × 50 connections was 200; 40 × 50 is 2,000, ten times as many. Each Postgres connection is a separate process with its own memory, so thousands of mostly idle connections hurt performance even when the limit allows them; that is why raising the limit to 2,000 is the wrong fix. A pooler such as PgBouncer multiplexes many client connections onto a few server ones, and smaller app pools keep the total in check. Removing the app pools makes it worse: every request pays to open a new connection. A read replica only takes reads, and each instance still opens its full pool.

items.prompt: After updating a product in the database, why do teams usually delete its cache key rather than write the new value into the cache?

choices.text: Two concurrent writers can set the cache out of order, leaving an old value in place
A deleted key is repopulated with a fresh TTL, which a written value would not get
Deleting is faster in Redis than overwriting a key with a new serialised value
Writing to the cache would require a distributed transaction with the database

choices: Two concurrent writers can set the cache out of order, leaving an old value in place
A deleted key is repopulated with a fresh TTL, which a written value would not get
Deleting is faster in Redis than overwriting a key with a new serialised value
Writing to the cache would require a distributed transaction with the database

items.explanation: Picture writer A saving price 10 and writer B saving price 12, so the database ends at 12. If each then sets the cache, A's set can land after B's, and the cache holds 10 indefinitely while the database says 12. Deleting the key instead means the next read misses and fetches whatever the database holds now, so the order of the two deletes does not matter. Speed is not the reason: a delete and an overwrite cost about the same in Redis. A set can carry a TTL just as easily as a refill does. And no distributed transaction is involved either way; the problem is the order of two writes, not atomicity.

items.prompt: Users upload videos of up to 2 GB. Which design keeps that traffic off your API servers?

choices.text: The API hands out a short-lived pre-signed URL; the browser uploads straight to storage
Stream each upload through the API and write it into a binary column in the database
Raise the API's body-size limit and request timeout, then scale the API out to cope
Split the file into chunks in the browser and post all of the chunks to the API in parallel

choices: The API hands out a short-lived pre-signed URL; the browser uploads straight to storage
Stream each upload through the API and write it into a binary column in the database
Raise the API's body-size limit and request timeout, then scale the API out to cope
Split the file into chunks in the browser and post all of the chunks to the API in parallel

items.explanation: A pre-signed URL grants time-limited permission to write one object, so the 2 GB go from the browser to object storage while your API only authorises the upload and records the key. Streaming through the API into a binary column pushes every byte through your servers and bloats the database too. Raising the body limit and scaling out still sends all 2 GB through the API, so you pay for that capacity. Chunking in the browser only splits the same bytes: if the chunks are posted to the API, every one of them still passes through your servers.

items.prompt: The double grade lived for 14 days although a smoke test mounted the whole app. Why could that test never have caught it?

choices.text: It used fake timers that fire intervals synchronously and skip the updaters
It asserted on rendered text, and the duplicate grade changed no visible text
It ran in production mode, where React strips the countdown timer component
It mounted the app without main.tsx's StrictMode, so updaters ran only once

choices: It used fake timers that fire intervals synchronously and skip the updaters
It asserted on rendered text, and the duplicate grade changed no visible text
It ran in production mode, where React strips the countdown timer component
It mounted the app without main.tsx's StrictMode, so updaters ran only once

items.explanation: It mounted HashRouter and App without the StrictMode wrapper that main.tsx uses, so updaters were never double-invoked. The harness ran a different tree from the one users got. The fix mounts StrictMode in the harness like main.tsx, plus a regression test for exactly one grade per timeout.

items.prompt: An author adds a `tags` array to an existing drill step that was created after v2 shipped. `npm run content` and `npm test` both pass. What happened to learners who had ticked that step?

choices.text: Unaffected: tags are metadata and take no part in the step's stored key
Moved: their ticks follow the untagged twin of that drill in another module
Migrated automatically: migrate() rekeys progress on each page load
Orphaned: tags are part of the target, so the step got a new, unguarded key

choices: Unaffected: tags are metadata and take no part in the step's stored key
Moved: their ticks follow the untagged twin of that drill in another module
Migrated automatically: migrate() rekeys progress on each page load
Orphaned: tags are part of the target, so the step got a new, unguarded key

items.explanation: stepTarget returns `deck|tags` for a tagged drill, and the coverage test only guards the 195 v1 keys. Target-derived keys fixed insertion, but an in-place target change mints a new key silently (LT-15); 88 post-v1 keys are unguarded.

items.prompt: Why does the content build import `stepTarget` from app/src/lib/types.ts instead of re-implementing the target rule in the .mjs script?

choices.text: Because the roadmap JSON is parsed through the types declared in types.ts
So the uniqueness check runs on the exact key the app stores, with no drift
So the build runs faster by reusing the app's already-compiled bundle
Because a .mjs script has no way to switch over TypeScript union types

choices: Because the roadmap JSON is parsed through the types declared in types.ts
So the uniqueness check runs on the exact key the app stores, with no drift
So the build runs faster by reusing the app's already-compiled bundle
Because a .mjs script has no way to switch over TypeScript union types

items.explanation: validateRoadmap computes `${step.kind}:${stepTarget(step)}` per module; a copy could drift and let two steps share one tick unnoticed. One definition shared by app, build and generator means they cannot disagree about what a key is.

items.prompt: The rewritten Countdown stores a fixed `deadline` and compares `Date.now()` against it, instead of decrementing a counter on each interval tick. Which failure does that remove?

choices.text: Leaks: intervals are left uncleared after the countdown component unmounts
Timezone errors: the learner's local clock crosses midnight mid-question
Wasted renders: each tick re-renders, which the deadline version avoids
Drift: throttled background tabs fire intervals late, so a tick counter runs slow

choices: Leaks: intervals are left uncleared after the countdown component unmounts
Timezone errors: the learner's local clock crosses midnight mid-question
Wasted renders: each tick re-renders, which the deadline version avoids
Drift: throttled background tabs fire intervals late, so a tick counter runs slow

items.explanation: Counting ticks mixed 'what time is it' with 'what happens when time runs out'; browsers throttle timers in background tabs, so only a wall-clock comparison against a fixed deadline stays correct.

items.prompt: Under the v1 key `${stageId}/${moduleId}/${index}`, an author inserts a new step at position 1 of a module and ships. What do learners who had ticked steps in that module see?

choices.text: Each tick silently slides one step, and the new step shows old step 1's tick
The build fails, because two steps in the module now claim the same index key
The new step appears unticked, and each existing tick stays on its own step
Each tick in the module is cleared, because the module's step count changed

choices: Each tick silently slides one step, and the new step shows old step 1's tick
The build fails, because two steps in the module now claim the same index key
The new step appears unticked, and each existing tick stays on its own step
Each tick in the module is cleared, because the module's step count changed

items.explanation: The key encodes position, so progress stored under `.../1` now names a different step - every later tick slides onto the step before it, with no error anywhere. Editing content had silently become a storage-schema migration.

items.prompt: Several consumers process order events in parallel, but events for the same order must be handled in sequence. What is the usual approach?

choices.text: Partition by order id, so every event for one order reaches the same consumer in order
Let any consumer take any event, and sort the order's history in the database later
Add a timestamp to each event and have consumers sleep until earlier ones finish
Use one consumer for the whole queue, since that is the only way to keep any order

choices: Partition by order id, so every event for one order reaches the same consumer in order
Let any consumer take any event, and sort the order's history in the database later
Add a timestamp to each event and have consumers sleep until earlier ones finish
Use one consumer for the whole queue, since that is the only way to keep any order

items.explanation: Ordering is needed per key, not globally, so partitioning by order id (Kafka partitions, SQS FIFO message groups, Service Bus sessions) sends every event of one order to the same consumer in sequence while different orders still run in parallel. A single consumer for the whole queue does keep order, but throws away all throughput. Timestamps plus sleeping guarantee nothing: a consumer cannot know that an earlier event is still in flight, and clocks differ between machines. Sorting the history afterwards is too late, because a handler has already acted on OrderCancelled before OrderPlaced arrived.
